newsitem.title: UK: Christopher seeks "concrete" steps from Israel.
newsitem.headline: Christopher seeks "concrete" steps from Israel.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher pressed Israel on Saturday for "concrete steps" to advance Middle East peace after the psychological breakthrough of this week's Netanyahu-Arafat meeting.
He told reporters travelling with him on a five-day trip to Europe that he would take this line when he met Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy in London on Sunday.
Christopher will also be present when Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu meets President Bill Clinton in Washington on Monday.

Netanyahu resisted meeting Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat after his election victory last May. But the two leaders finally got together -- and shook hands -- last Wednesday on Israel's border with Gaza, one of several areas now admninistered by the Palestinians under a 1993 peace accord.
The United States had been intensely involved behind the scenes in persuading Netanyahu -- elected on a platform of much greater scepticism of peace moves with Arabs -- to meet Arafat.
Christopher said the first meeting had been "a very important psychological breakthrough".
"And now we'd like to see that translated into ... concrete steps to move forward in the actual (peace) process."
"There are a number of issues on the table and I hope there will be a momentum coming out of the meeting that will enable the parties to address these."
Although pressed by reporters, Christopher would only specify one step he would like to see taken.
He called for a "substantial easing" of Israel's closure of borders with the West Bank, a move that has imposed severe hardship on Palestinians by curtailing trade and access to jobs.

Netanyahu has indicated he would do this and Christopher acknowledged it was quite likely to happen, now that the Israeli leader and Arafat had talked face-to-face and Netanyahu could understand the difficulties caused by the closure.
One major outstanding issue was Israel's pledge to withdraw most of its troops from Hebron, an ancient town that is a key Palestinian centre but also has a few Jewish residents.
Netanyahu was heckled by hardliners at a stormy convention of his Likud party on Thursday because of his meeting with Arafat, long denounced as a "master terrorist" by the party.

In his speech to the convention, he vowed never to budge from Likud's traditional support for Jewish settlements in the West Bank and Gaza Strip and its rejection of the Palestinian goal of an independent state.
But he also slapped down his critics, declaring: "In battles for peace, as in battles in war, there is only one commander."

"On the principle of continuing this (peace) process according to our understanding and in the way we are steering it, all cabinet ministers will have to accept it, or they won't be ministers," he told Israel Television later.
